title: The War on Fat
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Richard Claydon uses the history of Ancel Keys and the war on dietary fat as a long case study in transformational leadership, opening with leaders who follow sound advice yet find both their metabolic health and their burden of leadership worsening. He shows how Keys turned a plausible scientific interpretation into a coordinated network of clinicians, associations, governments and manufacturers who could act on it. The case turns on consequences: manufacturers reformulated foods, the supply of added fats shifted toward vegetable oils, and heart-disease deaths fell for several reasons while obesity and metabolic syndrome rose, so nobody could trace which effects belonged to which intervention. He contrasts this with the distributed, argumentative metabolic-health movement of journalists, clinicians and self-experimenters, which lacks coordination but keeps asking questions the orthodoxy left open. The essay ends by asking what leadership means when the capacity to mobilise change outruns the capacity to understand the system being changed, and how anyone would know a success had created consequences they could no longer see.
points: Keys' achievement was less the science than connecting a plausible interpretation to a network of institutions able to act on it at scale.
A campaign aimed at one measurable target changed the food system in ways no architect directed, as each actor optimised its own objective.
Success on the chosen scorecard, falling coronary deaths, coexisted with deteriorating metabolic health, so progress on a measure is not progress on the system.
The metabolic-health challengers show distributed intelligence producing real discoveries and real exaggeration, without the means to coordinate institutional change.
The leadership question is what to do when capacity to mobilise change exceeds capacity to comprehend the system, and how to keep coherence for action while letting experiments challenge assumptions.
quotes: Why, despite following established advice about health and diet, am I becoming less metabolically healthy? And why, despite following established leadership practices, am I finding the burden of leadership increasingly difficult to manage?
His great achievement was to connect a plausible scientific interpretation to a network capable of acting upon it. What followed would eventually exceed the reach of any one scientist’s intention.

No single architect directed these changes. Different parts of the system pursued different objectives: lower measured saturated fat, longer shelf life, lower costs, better texture, regulatory compliance, consumer appeal or higher sales.

There is an irony here with consequences extending well beyond the original dietary debate. A campaign intended to improve health partly stimulated new expertise in making industrially reformulated foods pleasurable to eat.
The record exposes an important distinction between the intended objective of a transformation and the changes that actually occur within the system.
There was no second Ancel Keys. No single scientist emerged with a compelling alternative hypothesis, gathered the leading institutions behind it and set out to reorganise the world’s food supply.
A scientific hypothesis became a set of recommendations. The recommendations became institutional commitments. The commitments became commercial opportunities.
What happens when our ability to mobilise change exceeds our ability to comprehend the system we are changing?
